title: Troas and Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
summary: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece and then, to avoid a plot, returns by land with a group of companions. At Troas, during a long Sunday gathering, a young man named Eutychus falls from a window and is restored to life. Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus and gives them a moving farewell, recalling his ministry, warning them of wolves to come, and entrusting them to God and the word of his grace.
story: Paul has resolved to go to Jerusalem and then Rome (19:21), and this chapter begins that final movement. The Ephesus riot is behind him, and his long years of free travel and church planting are coming to an end. The speech at Miletus is the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to Christians, and it works as his farewell address, like Moses's in Deuteronomy or Jesus's at the Last Supper. It looks back over his ministry and forward to the dangers the church will face without him. The chapter's mood is heavy with foreboding: chains and afflictions await him, and his friends will not see his face again.
historical:
Paul's letters fill in what Acts compresses. After Ephesus he went to Macedonia (where he probably wrote 2 Corinthians) and then to Greece, meaning chiefly Corinth, for three months, where he most likely wrote Romans around AD 56 or 57. The companions listed in verse 4 come from the regions where Paul had planted churches, and many scholars think they were delegates carrying the collection Paul had organized among Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-27; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4; 2 Corinthians 8-9). Acts mentions that gift only in passing, later (24:17). The first-person we resumes in verse 5, at Philippi, where it had left off in chapter 16.

The voyage from Troas hugs the coast of Asia Minor, stopping at island and harbor towns in turn. Miletus, an old and famous Greek city, lay about thirty miles (50 kilometers) south of Ephesus by land, so the elders' trip to meet Paul would have taken some days. Paul wanted to reach Jerusalem for Pentecost, fifty days after Passover, when pilgrims from across the Jewish world would be present.
cultural:
The meeting at Troas on the first day of the week, to break bread, is one of the earliest clear references to Christians gathering on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, alongside 1 Corinthians 16:2. Since the first day was an ordinary working day in the Roman world, believers often met in the evening, which explains the lamps and the late hour. An upper room on the third story suggests an apartment building, where many city dwellers lived; lamp smoke and a crowded room help explain why a young man sitting in the window fell asleep.

In the Miletus speech, Paul uses three terms for the same leaders: elders (verse 17), overseers (verse 28, episkopoi, the word later translated bishops), and those who shepherd the church. Christians who favor rule by a group of elders and those who favor a distinct office of bishop both draw on this chapter; most agree that at this early stage the words elder and overseer describe the same people. Paul's reminder that he worked with his own hands reflects the Greek world's suspicion of traveling teachers who lived off their followers. His quotation of Jesus in verse 35 is a saying not found in any of the four Gospels, a reminder that the early church preserved words of Jesus beyond those written down.
literary: The chapter has a travel report (verses 1-16) with one story at its center, and a speech (verses 17-38). The speech has a clear shape: Paul looks back on his conduct (verses 18-21), looks ahead to what awaits him (verses 22-24), charges the elders to guard the flock (verses 25-31), and commits them to God with a final example (verses 32-35). It shares many words and themes with Paul's letters, among them serving the Lord with humility, finishing the course, the grace of God, and working to support himself, which is one reason scholars see it as the speech in Acts closest to the Paul of the letters. The ending is intimate and physical: kneeling in prayer, weeping, embracing, and walking together to the ship.

outline.t: Through Macedonia and Greece to Troas
Paul recalls his ministry and faces what awaits him
Committed to God and the word of his grace

doctrines.note: The church is a flock that belongs to God, bought at the highest price, and entrusted to shepherds who must first keep watch over themselves. Leadership is presented as service and vigilance, not status.
Paul says God purchased the church with His own blood (verse 28). The church exists because of the costly death of Christ, which Paul presents as God's own act of redemption.

Paul warns that false teachers will come from outside and even from within, drawing disciples after themselves. The safeguard he names is not a program but the word of His grace, which can build believers up.
Paul counts his life of no value to him compared with finishing his course. Suffering is expected, and faithfulness is measured by completing the task received from the Lord Jesus.

words.note: Episkopos, overseer, one who watches over others. It later became the title of a bishop, but here Paul uses it of the Ephesian elders, whom the Holy Spirit has made overseers. The emphasis falls on responsibility for the flock, not rank.

Poimaino, to shepherd, to tend a flock by feeding, guiding, and protecting it. The Old Testament often calls Israel's leaders shepherds and condemns those who fed themselves instead (Ezekiel 34). Jesus gave Peter the same charge (John 21:16).

Tapeinophrosune, humility, lowliness of mind. In Greek culture this was not usually a virtue, since it suggested servility. Christians made it one because of Christ, and Paul names it first in describing how he served the Lord.

christ: The Miletus speech is full of Christ even when it speaks about Paul. His ministry was received from the Lord Jesus, and its content was repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and the good news of God's grace. The church he entrusts to the elders is the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood, a statement of the cost of the cross. And Paul closes by quoting Jesus: It is more blessed to give than to receive. That saying, preserved nowhere else, sums up the self-giving pattern of Jesus's own life, and Paul offers his own work and generosity as a picture of it. The restoration of Eutychus at a Sunday gathering to break bread also quietly echoes the resurrection that the day commemorates.

hard.q: What does it mean that God purchased the church with His own blood?
hard.a:
The phrase in verse 28 is striking, since God as spirit has no blood. There are two questions, one about the text and one about the grammar. Some early manuscripts read the church of the Lord rather than the church of God, though most textual scholars prefer of God as the harder and better-attested reading. The grammar allows either with His own blood or with the blood of His own, meaning his own Son, and several modern translations offer the second in a footnote or the text.

If the phrase means God's own blood, it reflects the early Christian confession that Jesus is truly God, so that what Christ suffered in his human nature can be said of God the Son; the church later expressed this in its teaching on the one person of Christ, fully divine and fully human. If it means the blood of his own Son, it echoes the language of Romans 8:32, where God did not spare his own Son. Both readings affirm that the church was bought at the cost of Christ's death and that this was God's own act.

questions: Paul told the elders to keep watch over themselves before watching over the flock. Why does the order matter?
Paul measured his life by whether he finished the task he received from the Lord. What would it mean to measure your life that way?
The Ephesian elders wept because they would not see Paul again. What does their farewell show about the kind of love that grows in a church?
